title.abbrev: Post: Signed Agent Identity for Mail

front.title: Post: Signed, Verifiable Identity for Software Agents That Send Email

abstract.t: Software agents now send email, and a recipient has no reliable way to tell that a message was written by software, on whose behalf it was sent, or whether the domain it claims to come from stands behind it. This document specifies Post, version 0: an agent declaration carried in ordinary mail and authenticated by an aligned DKIM signature; a per-domain Ed25519 key discovered through DNS and HTTPS; a signed copy of the message in a header field, which a receiver verifies against that key; typed, structured data carried beside the human text; and the format of signed receipts; and a signed card per agent address. Everything specified here, except the signed receipt, is implemented and running in production; the rest is listed as future work.

note.name: About This Draft
note.t: This draft is written for the IETF 127 hackathon (14-15 November 2026). Its source, the test vectors in machine-readable form and the issue tracker are at https://github.com/pidgeon-ai/post.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: An email message written by a software agent looks like any other. A recipient, human or software, cannot tell from the message whether a person or a program wrote it, who is responsible for the program, or whether the claims in the message are the sending domain's or a forger's. DKIM and DMARC say that a domain handled a message; they say nothing about what kind of sender wrote it or for whom.

Two individual drafts propose header fields for part of this: "Agent Attribution Header Fields" defines Agent-of and Agent-attribution, and the "AI Content Disclosure Header" defines AI-Disclosure for HTTP. Work on agent identity in the WIMSE working group (, ) addresses workloads that call each other over HTTP, not mail.
Post builds on the first two and adds what a recipient needs to rely on them:

ol.li: An agent declaration, using those fields, that a sender emits and a receiver may trust only under a passing, aligned DKIM signature ().
A signing key per domain, discovered from DNS and HTTPS in the manner of MTA-STS (), and a signed card per agent address ().
A verification procedure with defined outcomes ().

Between two endpoints that both implement Post: a signed copy of the message (the "envelope"), carried in a header field, which binds the declared sender to the From address, the recipients, the text, any structured data and every attachment (); typed data; and receipts ().

section.t: Nothing here asks a recipient to change mail software. A receiver that implements none of it sees ordinary mail.

section.name: Scope of Version 0
section.t: This version specifies only what is implemented, plus the receipt format. In particular, it does not specify delivery over HTTPS between hosts, first-contact policy, end-to-end encryption or a client protocol; see .

section.name: Conventions and Terminology
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

dl.dd: Software that writes and sends messages, typically driven by a language model, on behalf of a person or an organisation.
One of "person", "agent" or "service" (software that is not an agent, such as a workflow or an application). No other value is defined.
A display string naming the party responsible for the sender, such as an organisation's name or its domain.
A domain that publishes a Post policy with at least one key () and signs envelopes for its addresses.
The operator of a signing domain's mail service. A host may serve many domains.
Any party that checks a message: a receiving mail system, a mail client, or the agent that reads the message.
A sender or receiver that implements this document.

section.t: base64url is Section 5 without padding. base64 is Section 4. Times are in UTC with a "Z" and no fractional seconds, unless stated otherwise.

section.name: The Agent Declaration
section.t: The agent declaration states, in ordinary header fields, that software wrote the message, what kind of software, and on whose behalf. It is readable by any receiver that understands the fields and requires nothing else of the receiving system.

section.name: Fields
section.t: A sender whose kind is "agent" or "service" emits all three of the following. A person sending a message an agent drafted (for example after approving it) emits only AI-Disclosure. A person sending their own message emits none of them.

dd.t: As defined in : an address-list naming who is responsible. A Post sender writes exactly one address. The address SHOULD be an alias at the DKIM signing domain that reaches the responsible party rather than a person's own mailbox, so the field does not publish a personal address. Its display name, when present, is the "on behalf of" value.
As defined in : base64 of a JSON object. That draft leaves the object's members to a future registry. Post defines these:

dl.dd: The integer 1.
The sender kind, "agent" or "service".
A string, or null when the sender declares no responsible party beyond the Agent-of address.
The host's domain name.
OPTIONAL. An HTTPS URL at which the host describes this message ().
OPTIONAL. The URL of the sending address's agent card ().

dd.t: A receiver MUST ignore members it does not recognise.

The field of , a Structured Field Dictionary , used here in mail with the same syntax. That draft defines the field for HTTP only; this document defines its use in a message header. Values a Post sender writes:

ul.li: mode=ai-originated: kind "agent".
mode=machine-generated: kind "service".
mode=ai-originated, reviewed-by="person": a person sent what an agent drafted.

section.t: The kind declared is the kind of what sent the message, not of the address. Software sending from an address that belongs to a person MUST declare "agent" (or "service"), never "person"; "person" means a person composed or approved the message.

A host MUST remove any of these three fields that a client supplied (for example in SMTP submission ) and emit only its own. Otherwise any user of the host could put a forged declaration under the host's signature.

section.name: Authentication by DKIM
section.t: The declaration is trustworthy only under a DKIM signature that covers it, from a domain that answers for it. A sender:

ul.li: MUST sign the message with DKIM , with an "h=" tag that includes Agent-of, Agent-attribution and AI-Disclosure (whichever are present), From, To, Cc, Subject, MIME-Version and Content-Type;
MUST use a signing domain ("d=") that is aligned, in the relaxed sense of , with the domain of the Agent-of address, as Section 1.2.1 requires;

SHOULD NOT rely on signing Message-ID or Date when a relay is known to rewrite them. (The implementation in omits both, because its outbound relay replaces the first and rewrites the second; the signature's "t=" tag dates it.)

section.t: That signature is separate from, and in addition to, any signature aligned with the From domain. A host that sends for many domains can answer for every declaration with one signing domain, its own, and the receiver learns from the alignment who is answering.

section.name: The Verify Link
section.t: When Agent-attribution carries "verify", the URL MUST be HTTPS, MUST be unguessable (the implementation uses 128 random bits) and SHOULD return a description of the message as the host recorded it: the kind, the on-behalf-of value, the From address and when it was sent. It MUST NOT return the subject, the body or the recipients, because the link travels with every forwarded copy. The page says the host sent a message; it does not say that the copy in hand is unchanged. That is what the signatures are for.

section.name: What a Receiver May Trust
section.t: A receiver MUST NOT act on Agent-of, Agent-attribution or AI-Disclosure unless ends in "signed". Given "signed", the receiver may rely on the host aligned with the Agent-of domain having stated the kind and on-behalf-of value. It has not learned that the statement is true: the host answers for it, as a domain answers for mail it signs.

section.name: Domain Keys and the Agent Card
section.t: A signing domain publishes Ed25519 public keys that sign envelopes () and agent cards (), and will sign receipts (). The pattern is MTA-STS's : a DNS record says the domain takes part, and an HTTPS document on a dedicated host name holds the policy.

section.name: The DNS Record
section.t: A TXT record at _post.<domain>:

The record says the domain signs. The id is a hint to refetch. A host that controls the domain's DNS SHOULD set it to the first 16 hexadecimal characters of the SHA-256 of the policy's exact bytes, so that it changes whenever the policy does. A host that does not control the DNS writes a fixed id once; nothing depends on it changing (). A receiver MUST treat a domain with no such record as not signing.

section.name: The Policy
section.t: The policy is served at https://post.<domain>/.well-known/post.json , never at the apex: the apex is usually somebody else's website, while post.<domain> can point at the host (for example by a CNAME), which then serves the policy and its TLS certificate. It is a JSON object:

dl.dd: REQUIRED. The string "post0".
OPTIONAL. Seconds a receiver may hold the policy; 86400 if absent.

dd.t: REQUIRED. An array of key objects, each with:

dl.dd: An opaque string naming the key, unique within the domain.
"Ed25519". A receiver MUST ignore a key with any other value.
The 32-byte public key , base64url.
When the key stops being valid. A receiver MUST ignore a key without a parseable value and MUST refuse a signature made with a key past it.
OPTIONAL. An object whose member "issuer" is the HTTPS URL of an OpenID Connect issuer for the domain's addresses. Its use is outside this document ().
Reserved for delivery over HTTPS (). A version 0 receiver MUST ignore them, and a host MUST NOT list in "features" anything it does not implement.

section.t: A receiver MUST ignore members it does not recognise. A receiver fetching a policy SHOULD use port 443 only, SHOULD NOT follow redirects, SHOULD refuse a host name that resolves to a private or loopback address, and SHOULD refuse a policy larger than 64 KiB.

section.name: Caching, Rotation and Refetching
section.t: A receiver clamps the policy's max_age to between 60 seconds and 7 days. It fetches the policy again in exactly these cases, checked in this order:

ol.li: It holds no policy for the domain.
Its copy is at least max_age seconds old.
The TXT record's id differs from the one it saw when it fetched.

A signature names a kid its copy does not hold, and its copy is at least 60 seconds old. A receiver MUST NOT refetch for an unknown kid more than once a minute per domain, and MUST refuse a kid still unknown after that.

section.t: Otherwise it verifies against the copy it holds. This rule is the discovery::decide function of the reference core ().

To rotate, a host publishes the new key beside the old one, signs with the new one at once, and sets the old key's not_after to max_age from now, after which it leaves the policy. A receiver holding the old policy meets an unknown kid and refetches. The TXT id is not needed for rotation, which is why a fixed id works for domains whose DNS the host does not hold.

section.name: Signatures
section.t: Every Post signature is pure Ed25519 over the exact bytes being signed. There is no canonical form: the bytes are produced once, signed, and carried and stored as they are; a receiver verifies the bytes it decodes. Two JSON texts equal as JSON but different as bytes do not share a signature.

Verification is strict. A receiver MUST reject a signature whose S is not less than the group order L, and MUST reject a public key or an R that is a point of small order. Plain verification as in accepts some such signatures; the test vectors in pin the line.

section.name: The Agent Card
section.t: The card is the newest part of this document (implemented 3 November 2026) and the most likely to change. Nothing in depends on it.

The declaration and the envelope give identity per message. The card gives it per address: a document, issued automatically by the address's host, that says what the address is and that a holder can check offline against the issuer's policy.

section.name: Format and Signature
section.t: A card is a JSON Web Signature in compact serialisation, with protected header {"alg": "EdDSA", "typ": "agent-card+jwt", "kid": <kid>}. The kid names a key in the issuer's policy (), and the signature is Ed25519 over the JWS signing input, verified strictly (). The typ keeps a card from being mistaken for another token signed by the same key. The payload is a JSON object:

dl.dd: https://post.<issuer domain>: the address's own domain when it signs, else the host's domain.
A stable identifier for the address that the issuer never reassigns, even if the address is deleted and created again.
Issued and expiry times, in seconds since the epoch. The implementation issues cards valid for a day and signs one afresh on each fetch.
"post0".
The address.

"agent" or "service". Never "person": a card says software speaks from the address. An address only people have sent from has no card, and a request for one is answered as for an address that does not exist. An address that software has sent from, declaring "agent", has a card of kind "agent" from its first such message on, so the card a message names can always be fetched.
As in the declaration; omitted when there is nothing to say.
{"domain", "verified"}: the account's domain and whether the host has verified control of it; omitted when there is none.
When the address was created.

What signs the address's mail, so a receiver knows what to expect: {"type": "post", "domain", "kid"} for the envelope key and {"type": "dkim", "domain", "selector"} for the signature over the declaration.
Coarse, never a count: "standing" is "new" (an address under 30 days old), "established" or "restricted" (suspended), and "since" is a month (YYYY-MM).
The card's permanent URL.

section.t: A card carries only what the address's own mail already says, or facts about its domain: never an owner, a member, or anything a mailbox holds.

section.name: Discovery and Checking

ul.li: From the mail: the Agent-attribution object carries a member "card", the card's URL, beside "verify" (the message's own page). It is under the declaration's DKIM signature.

From the address alone: GET https://post.<domain>/.well-known/post/card?address=<address> returns {"object": "agent_card", "url", "jws", "card"}, where card is the payload decoded for reading and jws is the authority.

section.t: To check a card, a receiver takes the domain from iss (the host name without its leading "post." label), obtains that domain's policy and the key named by kid (), verifies the signature, checks exp, and checks that address is the address it is asking about. A card from an issuer other than the address's own domain is the host's statement, not the domain owner's.
The address lookup lets anyone ask whether an address is an agent's. SMTP already says whether it exists and its mail says the rest; the implementation rate-limits the lookup per client address.

section.name: Revocation
section.t: An issuer revokes a card by withdrawing it: from then on a request for the card, by its URL or by address, is answered as for an address that does not exist (HTTP 404), and the card log records a "revoked" entry for its sub (). Revocation cannot be undone, and an issuer MUST NOT reuse a revoked card's sub. A host issuing for accounts () MUST NOT issue a card for a revoked card's address again, to anybody: a receiver that trusted the address would otherwise extend that trust to whoever holds it next. A domain issuing for its own addresses () SHOULD NOT; if it does, the card has a new sub and the log a new subject, so a receiver keyed on sub sees a stranger.

A receiver holding a copy may believe it until its exp, at most a day in the implementation. A receiver acting on a card for something that matters SHOULD fetch it afresh or check the log's head, rather than rely on a copy. Suspending an address is not revocation: its card stays, with reputation standing "restricted".

section.name: Issuance for a Domain the Host Does Not Hold
section.t: A host can issue cards for addresses on any domain, with no account, in the way ACME's DNS challenge issues certificates. The operator of the domain holds the signing key; the host holds only its public half and signs the cards.

ol.li: The operator makes an Ed25519 key. Its key id, wherever this document uses one for it (the policy's kid, the envelope's k, an HTTP signature's keyid), is its JWK thumbprint , base64url-encoded.

The operator claims the domain at the host, naming the public key, in a request signed by that key (, with the tag "pidgeon-id"). The host answers with the record that proves the claim: the domain's post TXT record () with an id that is the first 16 hexadecimal digits of SHA-256 over the UTF-8 string "post id claim", a NUL, the domain, a NUL and the key id.

Once that record is published, the domain is the key's. A claim made by anyone else, before or after, names another key and so another id, and never proves. Proving the domain again with a new key replaces the old key and every card issued under it.

The operator registers addresses at the domain, in requests signed by the domain's key. Each gets a card () whose iss is the host's domain, whose operator is the proved domain with verified true, and whose keys name the operator's key. The host signs it on each fetch, valid for a day, while the record stands, so a card renews itself and lapses when the record is removed.
The host serves the domain's policy, from the operator's public keys, at https://post.<domain> once the operator points that name at it. The policy carries no endpoint.

section.t: The operator's key signs the address's envelopes () and HTTP requests (). A receiver verifies them against the domain's policy, as for any domain.

section.name: Agent Requests over HTTP
section.t: An agent signs an HTTP request with HTTP Message Signatures in the profile of , so that a receiver that checks Web Bot Auth signatures needs nothing new. The implementation signs with alg "ed25519", tag "web-bot-auth", keyid the key's JWK thumbprint, and a validity of five minutes. It covers @method, @authority, @path, @query when there is one, Signature-Agent, From, and Content-Digest when there is a body.

ul.li: Signature-Agent is "https://post.<domain>", sent as a bare String, the form deployed verifiers read today; a receiver also accepts the Dictionary form the profile asks signers for.
From is the agent's address. A receiver treats it as the sender only when it is at the domain whose key verified the signature.

The domain's key directory, at https://post.<domain>/.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory, lists the same keys as its policy, as a JWK Set whose kids are their thumbprints. The implementation does not sign the directory response, since the host does not hold the keys.

section.t: A call to an MCP server over its HTTP transport is an HTTP request, and is signed the same way.

Post does not replace Web Bot Auth; it is one more way to find out who holds the key. A Web Bot Auth verifier checks a Post agent's request with nothing new: same profile, same key directory, same keyid. What Post adds sits beside the signature, not in it:

ul.li: An address. The covered From names one agent among many under one key, where Web Bot Auth names an operator.
The agent card (), found from that address: kind (agent or service), on_behalf_of, a verified operator domain, and a coarse standing.
One key for mail and HTTP. The envelope's k and the request's keyid are the same thumbprint, published in the policy and the key directory alike.

section.t: A grant () rides beside the signature in a Post-Grant field, which the signature covers like From.

section.name: A Card in an A2A Agent Card
section.t: An agent that publishes an A2A Agent Card can carry its Post identity in it with A2A's own mechanisms, so that an A2A client needs nothing new and a Post-aware one can check it:

ul.li: An entry in capabilities.extensions with uri https://pidgeon.ai/post/a2a/v0, required false, and params address, kind, on_behalf_of (when there is one), operator (the domain), card_url and card_jws (the card's compact JWS, which is the authority; the other members are for reading).

An entry in signatures (A2A's AgentCardSignature): JWS JSON form without the payload, over the RFC 8785 canonical form of the Agent Card without signatures, by the operator's key. The protected header has alg "EdDSA", kid the key's JWK thumbprint, and jku the domain's key directory (), which is a JWK Set.

section.t: The fields map as follows: the Post card's address and kind have no A2A counterpart and travel in the extension; operator corresponds to AgentProvider (organization, url), which A2A does not verify and the card does; the A2A card's name, description, skills and interfaces have no Post counterpart. A verifier checks the signature against the key at jku, then the card_jws against its issuer's policy, then that the card's address is at the domain whose key signed the A2A card.

A grant () is not part of an A2A Agent Card, which is public and names no customer. An A2A client sends it with the task instead: in the message's metadata, under the extension's uri, as {"grants": [<compact JWS>, ...]}.

section.name: The Card Log
section.t: A host that issues cards automatically can issue one for anybody, including a card that names somebody else. The card log makes every card the host issues public, so the impersonated party can find it, in the way Certificate Transparency makes every certificate public. It is an append-only Merkle tree whose heads the host signs; anyone can check that a card is in it and that the log only ever grew.
An entry records a change to a card subject, not a signed card, since cards are re-signed daily (). It is a JSON object in its canonical form , and its exact bytes are what the tree hashes:

dl.dd: "post0-log".
"issued" (the subject has a card, for the first time or again), "updated" (a logged member below changed), or "revoked" (it has none).
When the log saw the change , to the second.
As in the card. Every entry about one address carries the same sub.
The index of the subject's previous entry; omitted on its first.
As in the card; omitted on "revoked".
As in the card, except that a "post" key also carries "pub", the public key in base64url, so a key replaced under the same kid is a change the log shows. Omitted on "revoked".

section.t: The card's iat, exp, reputation, created_at and url are not logged: they change by the day or never.

The tree is that of , Section 2.1: a leaf hash is SHA-256 of 0x00 and the entry's bytes, an interior node SHA-256 of 0x01 and its children, and inclusion and consistency proofs are built and verified as Sections 2.1.3 and 2.1.4 say. The signed tree head is a checkpoint : three lines (the log's origin, its size in decimal, its root hash in base64) in a signed note with one Ed25519 signature , whose key name is the origin. The log's key is the log's identity and never rotates; a client pins it as a signed-note verifier key.
The implementation serves, with no credentials:

ul.li: GET /v1/log/head and, as text, GET /v1/log/checkpoint: the current checkpoint and verifier key.
GET /v1/log/entries?start=&end=: entries by index, each with its exact bytes.
GET /v1/log/proof?sub= (or index and tree_size): an inclusion proof against a checkpoint.
GET /v1/log/consistency?first=&second=: a consistency proof between two sizes.

section.t: A verifier given a card and an inclusion proof hashes the entry's bytes, checks that the entry's sub and claims are the card's, verifies the checkpoint with the pinned key, and verifies the proof against its root. The implementation's verifier returns that proof with its verdict. A monitor keeps the last checkpoint it verified, asks for a consistency proof each time the size grows, and reads the new entries; a card it did not expect, for a name it watches, is the alarm. The log is reconciled from the cards every five minutes, its maximum merge delay. The Card Log vectors are in .

section.name: Grants
section.t: Grants are newer than the card (implemented 4 November 2026) and the most likely part of this document to change.

The card says who an agent is and for whom it acts. A grant says what it may do: that a person or an organisation allowed this agent to act within a named scope, for one customer, account or order, with one recipient, until a time. A recipient that is about to act on an agent's request (a support desk changing a booking, a vendor issuing a refund) checks the grant before it acts.

section.name: Format and Signature
section.t: A grant is a JWS in compact serialisation, with protected header {"alg": "EdDSA", "typ": "agent-grant+jwt", "kid": <kid>}, signed and verified as a card is (). The typ keeps a grant from being taken for a card or another token signed by the same key. The payload:

dl.dd: https://post.<issuer domain>: the host that saw the grantor agree. The implementation signs with the key of the domain that signs the cards it issues itself.
The grant's identifier, which the issuer never reuses.
The agent's card sub ().
The agent's address.
Issued and expiry times, in seconds since the epoch. The implementation lets the operator cap the term, at most 366 days.
"post0".

{"type": "person", "email", "confirmed_by"}, where confirmed_by is "email" (the person followed a link the issuer sent to that address) or "session" (they were signed in to the issuer as it); or {"type": "organisation", "domain", "confirmed_by": "domain"}, a domain the issuer has verified, granted by an administrator of the account that holds it.

{"name", "label", "limit"?}: name is stable, for software ("bookings.manage"); label is what the grantor was shown ("manage your bookings"); limit is {"amount", "currency"}, an integer in the currency's minor units and an ISO 4217 code. Scopes are the operator's; this document defines none.
The domain the agent may act with. Omitted: any.
{"type", "id"}: type is "customer", "account" or "order", and id is in the recipient's own terms.
An https URL at the issuer that answers whether the grant still holds ().

section.name: Issuing
section.t: The operator of an agent defines the scopes its agents may ask for. The agent asks a person, by email address, for one scope, one subject and a term; the issuer makes a pending request and a consent page, which says, for example, "Acme's assistant wants to manage your bookings with Delta until 31 December 2026". The person answers there. Holding the page's address is not consent, since the operator holds it too: the person allows the grant only after following a link the issuer sends to the address asked, or while signed in to the issuer as that address. Only then does the issuer sign. An organisation grants its own agents directly. Either the grantor or the operator may revoke a grant at any time, and a revoked grant is never restored.

section.name: Carrying a Grant

ul.li: In mail: a Post-Grant header field per grant, whose value is the compact JWS. White space in the value is not part of it, so a sender may break the value at any point to fold the field; a receiver removes all white space.
In HTTP: a Post-Grant field, several grants separated by commas (a JWS contains none), covered by the request's signature ().
In an MCP call: under the key ai.pidgeon.post/grant in the request's _meta, as a compact JWS or a list of them.
In A2A: in the message's metadata ().

section.t: A receiver reads at most five grants from one message or request.

section.name: Checking a Grant
section.t: A grant on its own proves nothing about who presents it: it is a bearer statement until it is bound to a signature. A receiver accepts a grant only when all of the following hold, and reports the first that does not:

ol.li: It is a grant: a compact JWS with this typ and every member above ("malformed").
Its iss is an issuer the receiver checks grants from ("unknown_issuer"), and the signature verifies under the key kid names in that issuer's policy ("bad_signature").

The issuer holds it in force: given, not revoked ("revoked"), and the same grant ("not_found"). A receiver that is not the issuer asks the status URL, which answers {"object": "grant_status", "id", "status", "expires_at", "revoked_at"} with status "active", "revoked" or "expired", and 404 for a grant never given. The implementation's verifier reads its own record on every check, and its status URL is cached for at most thirty seconds, so a revocation is seen within a minute.
exp is in the future ("expired").
A signature on the same message or request verifies as an address (, ) ("sender_unverified"), and that address is the grant's agent, still holding the grant's sub ("wrong_agent").
Where the receiver knows where it arrived (the recipient's address, or the request's host), that is aud or under it ("wrong_audience").
Where the receiver knows which customer, account or order it is about to act on, that is subject.id ("wrong_subject").

section.t: A grant never changes the verdict on the sender; it is a separate answer about what the sender may do.

section.name: Verification
section.t: A receiver checks the two layers independently. Either may be absent; each has its own outcome.

ol.li: If the message has none of Agent-of, Agent-attribution and AI-Disclosure, the outcome is "absent".

Find DKIM signatures whose "h=" tag covers every instance of those fields that is present, and whose "d=" is aligned (relaxed) with the domain of the Agent-of address. A message with AI-Disclosure alone has no Agent-of to align with: any DKIM signature covering the field qualifies, and its "d=" names the party answering for it. If there is none, the outcome is "absent": the message claims a declaration that nobody answers for, and a receiver SHOULD say so.
Verify such a signature . If none verifies over the header fields, the outcome is "changed".

Read the facts only from the field instances the signature covered (in DKIM, the last instances). An instance outside the signature, such as a second Agent-of added in transit, MUST be ignored and SHOULD be reported.

If the body hash also verifies, the outcome is "signed", body "intact". If only the header fields were available (for example a pasted header section), it is "signed", body "not checked". If the body hash fails, the declaration is "signed" but the body is "changed", and a receiver MUST NOT treat the body as the sender's.

section.name: The Envelope
section.t: For a message with a Post-Envelope field, in this order, stopping at the first failure:

ol.li: Parse. Take the field; remove whitespace from each tag value; require v, d, k, s and m, and v equal to "post0". Otherwise: malformed.
Domain. d MUST equal, ignoring case, the domain of the From address. Otherwise: domain_mismatch.

Key. Obtain d's policy and the key named by k by the rules of . No TXT record: not_published. No usable policy: policy_unavailable. A kid still unknown: unknown_kid. A key past not_after: expired_key.
Signature. Decode m and s, and verify s over the bytes of m, strictly (). Otherwise: bad_signature.
Message. The bytes of m MUST be valid UTF-8 JSON with v "post0" and a sender.kind that is a sender kind. Otherwise: invalid_message.

li.t: Agreement with the MIME. The signed message MUST say what the MIME says, because the MIME is what will be shown and stored:

ul.li: sender.address equals the From address, ignoring case (sender_mismatch);
subject equals the decoded Subject (subject_mismatch);
to and cc, as sets and ignoring case, equal the To and Cc addresses (recipients_mismatch);
the set of attachment sha256 values equals the set of SHA-256 hashes of the files carried; a file the message does not list fails (attachment_mismatch).

section.t: If every step passes, the outcome is "pass", and the declared sender is the signed message's sender.kind and sender.on_behalf_of. Anything not checked above, the HTML alternative in particular, is not covered, and a receiver that has a "pass" SHOULD show the text rather than the HTML.
Without a Post-Envelope field the outcome is "none".

section.name: Combining the Outcomes

ul.li: Envelope "pass": the declared sender is the envelope's. It is the sending domain's own statement, and it is bound to the content.
Otherwise, declaration "signed": the declared sender is the declaration's, stated by the host aligned with the Agent-of domain.
Otherwise: no declared sender. The receiver records the kind and on-behalf-of as unknown, not as "person". Mail arriving this way from ordinary email is said to have origin "smtp".

section.t: A failed envelope is evidence that something is wrong. A receiver MUST NOT treat it as "pass", and MAY refuse the message.

"pass" proves that the domain wrote this content for these To and Cc recipients. It does not prove that this copy was sent to this receiver (), and it does not replace DMARC as the test of whether the From domain sent this copy.

section.name: Between Post Endpoints
section.t: When both ends implement Post, the same message carries more than either end gets from ordinary mail. Version 0 specifies what an endpoint delivers over ordinary SMTP, or by any equivalent hand-off between two endpoints run by the same host; delivery over HTTPS between hosts is future work.

section.name: Knowing the Other End Speaks Post
section.t: A sender learns that a recipient's domain signs from the _post record (). Version 0 gives no stronger signal: a domain that signs is not thereby promising to verify. A host may know more about addresses it hosts itself.

section.name: The Signed Envelope
section.t: A signing domain signs each message it sends as a JSON document, the "message", and carries it with the signature in a header field. A receiver that holds the domain's key can then check the declared sender and the content against the domain's signature, with no DKIM involved and no dependence on how relays rewrite the MIME.

section.name: The Message
section.t: A JSON object, UTF-8, serialised once. Members:

dl.dd: "post0".
An opaque string of at most 64 characters, unique per sending domain.
An object: "id", set by whoever starts the conversation and never changed; and "parent", the id of the message replied to, when it is a reply.
An object: "address", the From address; "kind", the sender kind; and "on_behalf_of", present only when the sender declares one. These are the same values as the agent declaration's ().
Arrays of addresses, as in the To and Cc fields. Bcc recipients never appear.
When the message was written.
The Subject, decoded.

ul.li: exactly one text part: {"role":"text", "type":"text/plain", "body": <the text>};
one attachment part per file: {"role":"attachment", "type": <media type>, "name": <file name>, "sha256": <hex>, "size": <octets>}.

section.t: The text part is written for a person. A receiving agent MUST treat it as untrusted content to read, never as instructions. HTML is not part of the message and nothing vouches for it.
The message carries files by hash only: at the SMTP border the bytes travel in the MIME beside it.

section.name: The Post-Envelope Header Field
section.t: The field's value is a list of tag=value pairs as in DKIM Section 3.2:
section.sourcecode: post-envelope = "Post-Envelope:" FWS env-tags CRLF env-tags = env-tag *( ";" FWS env-tag ) [";"] env-tag = tag-name "=" tag-value ; RFC 6376, Section 3.2

dl.dd: "post0".
The signing domain. It MUST be the domain of the From address.
The kid of the key that signed.
The Ed25519 signature over the message bytes, base64url.
The message bytes, base64url.

section.t: A sender breaks the values of s and m into runs (the implementation uses 76 characters) separated by spaces so the field can be folded; a receiver removes all whitespace from every value before using it, as from a DKIM "b=" tag. A receiver MUST ignore tags it does not recognise.

A sender SHOULD NOT emit the field when the message is larger than 24 KiB before encoding: some mail systems discard header text past 100 KB, which would leave an envelope that cannot be verified. Such a message goes out without one, as does mail from a domain that does not sign.

section.name: Typed Data in MIME
section.t: A message may carry one piece of structured data beside its text: a "schema", an http or https URL of at most 900 characters naming what the data is (for example https://schema.org/Offer), and a "body", any JSON value of at most 64 KiB serialised. It travels:

ul.li: in the envelope, as the data part;

in the MIME, as an alternative inside the message's multipart/alternative, after any HTML alternative and before any calendar part, with type application/vnd.post+json, parameters charset=utf-8 and schema="<URL>", and base64 transfer encoding.

section.t: It is an alternative, not an attachment, so a client that does not understand it shows the text or HTML. A receiver lifts the first such part whose content is JSON and whose schema is an http(s) URL into the message's data; anything else stays an attachment.

The schema is a label a receiver may check, not something version 0 validates. Data is parsed as data. A receiving agent MUST NOT treat it as instructions, and a screening system that reads prose for prompt injection has no reason to read it.

section.name: Delivery
section.t: A sender delivers one copy per recipient, carrying the Post-Envelope field, the typed data alternative and the agent declaration. A receiving endpoint runs before storing anything. On "pass" it stores the copy with the declared sender from the envelope and the text (not the HTML), and reports that the signature passed. On failure it MUST NOT store the copy as verified.
A receiver keeps the original bytes of a delivered copy where it can, so the signature can be checked again later.
The Message-ID SHOULD be the same on every recipient's copy, so a reply from an ordinary mail client threads back to the conversation.

section.name: Receipts
section.t: A receipt tells a sender what happened to a message after it reached the recipient's endpoint. Kinds:

dl.dd: The copy is in the recipient's mailbox.
The receiving agent or person opened it. A recipient MUST NOT send it unless the recipient's mailbox has opted in, and MAY refuse it without saying why. It is off by default.
The recipient's conversation passed from software to a person.
The message could not be delivered.

section.t: A receiving endpoint sends each kind at most once per received copy.

section.name: The Receipt
section.t: A JSON object, signed as exact bytes like the message:

dl.dd: "post0".
The id of the message ().
The sending domain. Ids are unique per sending domain only, so the pair names the message.
The address whose copy this is.
The receipt kind.
When it happened.

section.t: The recipient's domain signs the bytes with a key from its own policy. A sender that keeps the bytes and the signature can show a third party that the recipient's domain confirmed the event.

section.name: Carrying a Receipt
section.t: A receipt travels as a JSON object with members "v" ("post0"), "d" (the recipient's domain), "kid", "receipt" (the receipt bytes, base64url) and "sig" (the signature, base64url). A receiver of a receipt verifies it as in steps 3 and 4, against d's policy, and checks that recipient's domain is d.
How a receipt reaches the sender is outside version 0; between addresses on one host it is an internal event. Over HTTPS between hosts it is future work ().

section.name: Names on the Wire
section.t: These identifiers carry the protocol's name:

tr.td: Version string in every object and record

section.name: Implementation Status
section.t: This section is to be removed before publication, as describes.

Pidgeon, an email service for people and software agents, implements everything in this document except the signed receipt (receipts are emitted unsigned, in the receipt's shape, as events to the sender). On 3 November 2026 the agent declaration was on 565 of 984 messages sent in the previous 7 days. Every message sent through the API from a signing domain carries Post-Envelope, unless it is over the size limit of ; messages from a user's own mail client by SMTP submission carry none. Between two Pidgeon addresses on signing domains, copies are delivered directly and verified by before they are stored; a copy that fails is refused and sent as ordinary mail.
The core is "post-core", in Rust (Apache-2.0), with a WebAssembly binding: Ed25519 signing and strict verification, and the refetch rule of . The test vectors in are produced from the running code.

Pidgeon also runs a public checker for the declaration, which reports the outcomes of for a pasted message, and of for a signed request. It issues cards for domains it does not host (); the operator's side is "@pidgeon-ai/id" (Apache-2.0), a command line and the signing library, over the same post-core.

Grants () are issued for addresses the implementation hosts, through its consent page, and checked by the same public checker; "@pidgeon-ai/id" carries them in mail and HTTP. It issues none yet for domains it does not host, and does not check grants from other issuers.

Known limits of the implementation: its inbound path from ordinary email does not yet verify Post-Envelope fields from other domains (the remote fetch of exists but is not called there); the DKIM signature over the declaration is the host's (d=pidgeon.email), not a second one from a customer's domain; and no receiver other than Pidgeon is known.

section.name: A Signature Is Not a Truth
section.t: The declaration and the envelope prove who stated something, not that it is true. A domain that lies about its sender's kind is caught only by the reputation of the domain that signed. Receivers SHOULD treat the signing domain, not the declaration, as the accountable party.

section.name: Forged Declarations
section.t: Agent-of and its companions are ordinary header fields anybody can write. They are worth nothing without , and a host that signs for many users MUST strip client-written instances (), or its signature would cover a forgery.

section.name: Replay
section.t: The envelope binds the content and the To and Cc recipients, but Bcc recipients are legitimately absent from it, so a receiver cannot tell a copy sent to it by Bcc from a captured message replayed to it. Version 0 has no freshness on the envelope: created_at is when the message was written, and a message may be retried for days. A receiver SHOULD NOT treat an envelope "pass" alone as proof that the From domain sent this copy to it; DMARC answers that question for mail that arrives by SMTP. The implementation trusts "pass" as sender authentication only for copies handed over directly by its own sending path, and ignores Post-Envelope on mail that arrives over SMTP. Binding a delivery to its recipients and a time is future work ().

section.name: Key Compromise and Revocation
section.t: Revocation is never instant. A stolen key is usable until the host removes it from its policy and every receiver's copy expires, at most the clamped max_age (7 days), and never past the key's not_after. Hosts SHOULD keep max_age short while withdrawing a key. The unknown-kid refetch is rate-limited so that an attacker cannot make a receiver fetch a policy on every message.

section.name: Fetching Policies
section.t: A policy fetch is a request a sender can make a receiver perform. The limits in (port 443, no redirects, no private addresses, a size cap) prevent its use against the receiver's own network. A policy is trusted only as far as the TLS certificate for post.<domain> and the domain's DNS are.

section.name: Content Written for People, Read by Software
section.t: The text part and the HTML are untrusted input. A receiving agent MUST NOT follow instructions found in them, whether or not the envelope passes: a signature says who wrote the text, not that it is safe. Typed data is parsed as data.

section.name: Signature Malleability
section.t: Strict Ed25519 verification () ensures one message has one valid signature per key, and that a weak key cannot make a forged signature pass. Implementations that use a library's default verification SHOULD check it against the vectors.

ul.li: Agent-of names a responsible party. It SHOULD be an alias rather than a person's mailbox. A host SHOULD NOT derive on_behalf_of from a person's name or address unless that person chose to publish it; the implementation uses an organisation name an owner set, else a verified domain, else nothing.
The verify link travels with every forward. It MUST NOT reveal the subject, body or recipients ().
The envelope repeats the To and Cc addresses and the text in a header field. It reveals nothing a recipient does not already have, but mail systems that log header fields will log it.
A read receipt reveals behaviour. It is off by default and opt-in per mailbox.

A grant names its grantor's email address and a customer, account or order, and travels to the recipient named in aud, who already knows both. The grantor sees that before agreeing. The status URL answers only for a grant that was given, by an identifier only a holder of the grant has, and says nothing of grantor, scope or subject.
A policy fetch tells the sending domain's host that some receiver is checking its mail, and roughly when. Caching limits this to once per max_age per receiver.

section.name: Message Header Fields
section.t: IANA is asked to register in the "Provisional Message Header Field Names" registry :

dl.dd: Post-Envelope
mail
provisional
this document,

section.t: and Post-Grant, with applicable protocol "mail", status provisional, referring to ; the same name in the "Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) Field Name Registry" , status provisional;

and AI-Disclosure, with applicable protocol "mail", status provisional, referring to for syntax and this document, , for its use in mail. Agent-of and Agent-attribution are left to , which requests no registration yet.

section.name: Well-Known URI
section.t: IANA is asked to register "post.json" in the "Well-Known URIs" registry , status provisional, referring to . The card lookup () uses "post/card"; whether it becomes a second registration or moves under one name is open.

section.name: Media Type
section.t: The media type application/vnd.post+json is to be registered in the vendor tree , with required parameter "schema" (an http or https URL) and optional "charset" ("utf-8").

section.name: Underscored DNS Node Name
section.t: IANA is asked to add "_post", RR type TXT, to the "Underscored and Globally Scoped DNS Node Names" registry , referring to .

section.name: Agent-attribution Members
section.t: When the registry anticipated by exists, the members in are to be registered in it.

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.

front.title: Date and Time on the Internet: Timestamps

abstract.t: This document defines a date and time format for use in Internet protocols that is a profile of the ISO 8601 standard for representation of dates and times using the Gregorian calendar.

front.title: The Base16, Base32, and Base64 Data Encodings

abstract.t: This document describes the commonly used base 64, base 32, and base 16 encoding schemes. It also discusses the use of line-feeds in encoded data, use of padding in encoded data, use of non-alphabet characters in encoded data, use of different encoding alphabets, and canonical encodings. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

This document specifies the Internet Message Format (IMF), a syntax for text messages that are sent between computer users, within the framework of "electronic mail" messages. This specification is a revision of Request For Comments (RFC) 2822, which itself superseded Request For Comments (RFC) 822, "Standard for the Format of ARPA Internet Text Messages", updating it to reflect current practice and incorporating incremental changes that were specified in other RFCs. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) permits a person, role, or organization that owns the signing domain to claim some responsibility for a message by associating the domain with the message. This can be an author's organization, an operational relay, or one of their agents. DKIM separates the question of the identity of the Signer of the message from the purported author of the message. Assertion of responsibility is validated through a cryptographic signature and by querying the Signer's domain directly to retrieve the appropriate public key. Message transit from author to recipient is through relays that typically make no substantive change to the message content and thus preserve the DKIM signature.
This memo obsoletes RFC 4871 and RFC 5672. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

This document describes elliptic curve signature scheme Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA). The algorithm is instantiated with recommended parameters for the edwards25519 and edwards448 curves. An example implementation and test vectors are provided.

front.title: The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format

abstract.t: JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a lightweight, text-based, language-independent data interchange format. It was derived from the ECMAScript Programming Language Standard. JSON defines a small set of formatting rules for the portable representation of structured data.
This document removes inconsistencies with other specifications of JSON, repairs specification errors, and offers experience-based interoperability guidance.
This memo defines a path prefix for "well-known locations", "/.well-known/", in selected Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) schemes.
In doing so, it obsoletes RFC 5785 and updates the URI schemes defined in RFC 7230 to reserve that space. It also updates RFC 7595 to track URI schemes that support well-known URIs in their registry.

This document describes a set of data types and associated algorithms that are intended to make it easier and safer to define and handle HTTP header and trailer fields, known as "Structured Fields", "Structured Headers", or "Structured Trailers". It is intended for use by specifications of new HTTP fields.
This document obsoletes RFC 8941.

front.title: Domain-Based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC)

abstract.t: This document describes the Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) protocol.

DMARC permits the owner of an email's Author Domain to enable validation of the domain's use to indicate the Domain Owner's or Public Suffix Operator's message handling preference regarding failed validation and to request reports about the use of the domain name. Mail-receiving organizations can use this information when evaluating handling choices for incoming mail.
This document obsoletes RFCs 7489 and 9091.

front.title: CFRG Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) and Signatures in JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE)

abstract.t: This document defines how to use the Diffie-Hellman algorithms "X25519" and "X448" as well as the signature algorithms "Ed25519" and "Ed448" from the IRTF CFRG elliptic curves work in JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE).

This document describes a mechanism for creating, encoding, and verifying digital signatures or message authentication codes over components of an HTTP message. This mechanism supports use cases where the full HTTP message may not be known to the signer and where the message may be transformed (e.g., by intermediaries) before reaching the verifier. This document also describes a means for requesting that a signature be applied to a subsequent HTTP message in an ongoing HTTP exchange.

This document defines HTTP fields that support integrity digests. The Content-Digest field can be used for the integrity of HTTP message content. The Repr-Digest field can be used for the integrity of HTTP representations. Want-Content-Digest and Want-Repr-Digest can be used to indicate a sender's interest and preferences for receiving the respective Integrity fields.
This document obsoletes RFC 3230 and the Digest and Want-Digest HTTP fields.

The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is a stateless application-level protocol for distributed, collaborative, hypertext information systems. This document describes the overall architecture of HTTP, establishes common terminology, and defines aspects of the protocol that are shared by all versions. In this definition are core protocol elements, extensibility mechanisms, and the "http" and "https" Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) schemes.
This document updates RFC 3864 and obsoletes RFCs 2818, 7231, 7232, 7233, 7235, 7538, 7615, 7694, and portions of 7230.

front.title: Registration Procedures for Message Header Fields

abstract.t: This specification defines registration procedures for the message header fields used by Internet mail, HTTP, Netnews and other applications. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

This memo splits message submission from message relay, allowing each service to operate according to its own rules (for security, policy, etc.), and specifies what actions are to be taken by a submission server.
Message relay is unaffected, and continues to use SMTP over port 25.
When conforming to this document, message submission uses the protocol specified here, normally over port 587.
This separation of function offers a number of benefits, including the ability to apply specific security or policy requirements. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: Media Type Specifications and Registration Procedures

abstract.t: This document defines procedures for the specification and registration of media types for use in HTTP, MIME, and other Internet protocols. This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice.

front.title: Improving Awareness of Running Code: The Implementation Status Section

abstract.t: This document describes a simple process that allows authors of Internet-Drafts to record the status of known implementations by including an Implementation Status section. This will allow reviewers and working groups to assign due consideration to documents that have the benefit of running code, which may serve as evidence of valuable experimentation and feedback that have made the implemented protocols more mature.

This process is not mandatory. Authors of Internet-Drafts are encouraged to consider using the process for their documents, and working groups are invited to think about applying the process to all of their protocol specifications. This document obsoletes RFC 6982, advancing it to a Best Current Practice.

SMTP MTA Strict Transport Security (MTA-STS) is a mechanism enabling mail service providers (SPs) to declare their ability to receive Transport Layer Security (TLS) secure SMTP connections and to specify whether sending SMTP servers should refuse to deliver to MX hosts that do not offer TLS with a trusted server certificate.

This specification defines a protocol for an HTTP- and JSON-based Security Token Service (STS) by defining how to request and obtain security tokens from OAuth 2.0 authorization servers, including security tokens employing impersonation and delegation.

front.title: Scoped Interpretation of DNS Resource Records through "Underscored" Naming of Attribute Leaves

abstract.t: Formally, any DNS Resource Record (RR) may occur under any domain name. However, some services use an operational convention for defining specific interpretations of an RRset by locating the records in a DNS branch under the parent domain to which the RRset actually applies. The top of this subordinate branch is defined by a naming convention that uses a reserved node name, which begins with the underscore character (e.g., "_name"). The underscored naming construct defines a semantic scope for DNS record types that are associated with the parent domain above the underscored branch. This specification explores the nature of this DNS usage and defines the "Underscored and Globally Scoped DNS Node Names" registry with IANA. The purpose of this registry is to avoid collisions resulting from the use of the same underscored name for different services.

Messaging applications are increasingly making use of end-to-end security mechanisms to ensure that messages are only accessible to the communicating endpoints, and not to any servers involved in delivering messages. Establishing keys to provide such protections is challenging for group chat settings, in which more than two clients need to agree on a key but may not be online at the same time. In this document, we specify a key establishment protocol that provides efficient asynchronous group key establishment with forward secrecy (FS) and post-compromise security (PCS) for groups in size ranging from two to thousands.

JSON Web Signature (JWS) represents content secured with digital signatures or Message Authentication Codes (MACs) using JSON-based data structures. Cryptographic algorithms and identifiers for use with this specification are described in the separate JSON Web Algorithms (JWA) specification and an IANA registry defined by that specification. Related encryption capabilities are described in the separate JSON Web Encryption (JWE) specification.

front.title: Handling Long Lines in Content of Internet-Drafts and RFCs

abstract.t: This document defines two strategies for handling long lines in width-bounded text content. One strategy, called the "single backslash" strategy, is based on the historical use of a single backslash ('\') character to indicate where line-folding has occurred, with the continuation occurring with the first character that is not a space character (' ') on the next line. The second strategy, called the "double backslash" strategy, extends the first strategy by adding a second backslash character to identify where the continuation begins and is thereby able to handle cases not supported by the first strategy. Both strategies use a self-describing header enabling automated reconstitution of the original content.

Public Key Infrastructure using X.509 (PKIX) certificates are used for a number of purposes, the most significant of which is the authentication of domain names. Thus, certification authorities (CAs) in the Web PKI are trusted to verify that an applicant for a certificate legitimately represents the domain name(s) in the certificate. As of this writing, this verification is done through a collection of ad hoc mechanisms. This document describes a protocol that a CA and an applicant can use to automate the process of verification and certificate issuance. The protocol also provides facilities for other certificate management functions, such as certificate revocation.

Cryptographic operations like hashing and signing need the data to be expressed in an invariant format so that the operations are reliably repeatable. One way to address this is to create a canonical representation of the data. Canonicalization also permits data to be exchanged in its original form on the "wire" while cryptographic operations performed on the canonicalized counterpart of the data in the producer and consumer endpoints generate consistent results.

This document describes the JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS). This specification defines how to create a canonical representation of JSON data by building on the strict serialization methods for JSON primitives defined by ECMAScript, constraining JSON data to the Internet JSON (I-JSON) subset, and by using deterministic property sorting.

front.title: HTTP Message Signatures for Automated Traffic

abstract.t: This document describes version 2.0 of the Certificate Transparency (CT) protocol for publicly logging the existence of Transport Layer Security (TLS) server certificates as they are issued or observed, in a manner that allows anyone to audit certification authority (CA) activity and notice the issuance of suspect certificates as well as to audit the certificate logs themselves. The intent is that eventually clients would refuse to honor certificates that do not appear in a log, effectively forcing CAs to add all issued certificates to the logs.
This document obsoletes RFC 6962. It also specifies a new TLS extension that is used to send various CT log artifacts.
Logs are network services that implement the protocol operations for submissions and queries that are defined in this document.

front.title: Workload Identity in a Multi System Environment (WIMSE) Architecture

section.name: Future Work
section.t: Designed, not implemented, and so not specified here:

ul.li: Delivery over HTTPS between hosts. One request per recipient domain to the policy's endpoint, carrying the message and a second signed object, the delivery, which names the recipients at that domain (Bcc included) and a send time, binding the message to its recipients and giving it freshness; with defined responses and idempotency on (sending domain, id).
Upgrade from SMTP. A sender that finds a recipient domain's record delivers over HTTPS instead.
First contact. What an unknown sender must bring: open, known contacts only, or an introduction signed by a domain the recipient knows.
Attachments by capability URL, fetched by the recipient before it reports delivered, and an "accepted" receipt.

Signing in with an address. The policy's identity.issuer as an OpenID Connect issuer for the domain's addresses, including OAuth token exchange in which the token names the person as sub and the agent as act (running at Pidgeon; to be specified separately).
The agent card, final (): cards for agents on hosts other than the implementation's, and a public verification API.
A second DKIM signature over the declaration from the customer's own domain.
End-to-end encryption with MLS , between mailboxes. Version 0 reserves the message member "enc"; a version 0 receiver rejects a message that carries it.
Threading. Deriving Message-ID, In-Reply-To and References from the message's id and thread.

section.name: Notes for a Second Implementation
section.t: A receiver that verifies envelopes needs: an Ed25519 library with strict verification, a DNS TXT lookup, an HTTPS client, a JSON parser and a MIME parser. It does not need a JSON canonicaliser. Points that are easy to get wrong:

ul.li: Verify the decoded bytes of m. Never re-serialise the parsed JSON and verify that.
Remove whitespace from every tag value before decoding: the field is folded.
base64url without padding for Post-Envelope, the policy's keys and receipts; ordinary base64 for Agent-attribution.
Compare the signed text with the text/plain body after CRLF to LF and trimming trailing whitespace; compare recipients as case-insensitive sets.
Refuse S >= L and small-order points. The vectors in fail under a lax verifier.
Rate-limit unknown-kid refetches per domain, across all of your processes.

section.t: A conformant receiver: verifies every valid vector; refuses every vector marked invalid; on the message in reaches "pass" for the envelope given the sender's policy, and "signed" with body "intact" for the declaration given the DKIM record; and reaches domain_mismatch on the refusal vector that changes d.

section.name: Ed25519 Vectors
section.t: The file ed25519.json, published with post-v0.json, holds RFC 8032's Section 7.1 tests 1 to 3, a protocol message and delivery signed with the seed 0x00..0x1f, a UTF-8 vector, and five refusals: the same JSON with a number written differently (1240.50 as 1240.5), a changed message, a wrong key, S + L (non-canonical S), and the identity point as key and R with S = 0 (passes plain RFC 8032 verification for any message). A conformant verifier accepts exactly those marked valid.

section.name: Test Vectors
section.t: Every value below is in the file post-v0.json at https://github.com/pidgeon-ai/post, which is authoritative: this appendix is generated from it, and long values are broken into runs of 64 characters for display. Whitespace is not part of any value. Seeds are Ed25519 private keys , which no real domain uses.

section.name: Discovery
section.t: The TXT record at _post.acme.example:
The policy served at https://post.acme.example/.well-known/post.json, exactly (it ends with a line feed). Its SHA-256, in hex, begins with the TXT record's id:

section.name: The Signed Message
section.t: The message bytes, UTF-8, shown on one line per field for display only; the signed bytes contain no line breaks and no spaces outside strings:
